messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] densities to build up a population model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Antonela, (list,)

Yes, I think you can use estimates of population density over time to
estimate population growth rate.  You could assume the estimated
population density follows a log-normal distribution; Distance provides
the relevant estimated mean and standard deviation.

A few considerations:

- Conventional distance sampling uses a hybrid of design-based and
model-based methods, and the model-based part (for estimating the
detection function parameters) uses maximum likelihood.  So, there's
something of a mis-match in paradigms if you then use this as the input
to a Bayesian trend model.  Not a big deal so long as you acknowledge
where the inputs came from; alternatively you could take a fully
Bayesian approach to the distance sampling data (at the cost of having
to make assumptions about the distribution of animals within the study
area, and having to specify priors on the various model parameters).

- Depending on how you do your analysis, the estimates of population
density over time might not be independent -- for example if they share
detection function parameters.  You should account for this in your
population modelling.  One of my PhD students, Rick Camp, is doing just
such a thing at present, I can put you in touch off the list if you want
more details.

Best wishes, Len Thomas

messages.subject: Combining Point Surveys
messages.body_plain:
I am analyzing some data collected using a point survey for common ravens.  20 points are surveyed over the course of a day and distances to observed groups of ravens are estimated at each point. It takes ~ 10 hours to run the survey. The survey is run once or twice weekly for 8 weeks, and has been repeated for 5 years.  I suspect that detectability does not change across the survey season, but some of the ravens are nomadic, so the density may vary from week to week (or day to day).  A challenge is that the number of clusters observed for any given survey is small, between 10 and 20 clusters. I understand that this number is small, and often when I look at the resulting plots from running a single observation date I can tell that no significant fitting is done given the small number of observations, often at similar distances.

My question is this:  Can I pool the data across a season to get a measure of detectability (p), then use that estimate of p to estimate numbers for the individual sample dates?  In the end I would like a time-series of density estimates for each of the seasons.

Thanks for any help.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Combining Point Surveys
messages.body_plain:
Hi Grant,

Short answer: yes!

Since you're interested in seasonal estimates of density then you can
estimate probability of detection at the level of season (so long as
there are enough samples), and any variation in detectability at "lower"
levels (i.e., between surveys within season, or between animals within
surveys) will not bias the seasonal estimates unless it is extreme, due
to the "pooling robustness" nature of distance sampling detection
function estimators. (So long as you use a flexible detection function
fitting algorithm, like the one in Distance, which uses the flexible key
function + adjustments-as-needed algorithm.)

You do seem to have enough samples, as you have around 15 clusters per
survey and around 12 surveys per season so around 180 samples per
survey.  Guidelines in the 1993 and 2001 books suggest around 90-120
samples are sufficient; none of us like cookbook numbers, but that's
intended to give some guidance on how many might be needed to get
reliable results for a "reasonable" detection function (see later) and
also have some chance of diagnosing any issues in the data.  By
"reasonable" I mean with a fairly wide shoulder (say g(x)=1 or close to
it for x < 0.2 * w where w is your truncation distance) and little or no
rounding of distances.  Point transects can be quite sensitive to things
like rounding, particularly of close by distances.

How might you structure this for analysis in Distance?  You could make
the season the stratum, and make the point the sample, pooling all
detections for each point over multiple surveys within a season into the
same sample record and setting the effort field to be the number of
surveys per season for that point.  Assuming you're using Distance for
Windows, you want to tick the options in Model Definition | Estimate to
Estimate detection function by stratum (assuming your season is set up
as the stratum); you also want density by stratum.

Another alternative for the detection function would be an MCDS
analysis, where you use season as a covariate or, perhaps better, any
other relevant covariates that you think affect detectability seasons.
You can use AIC to tell you whether such covariate analyses are "better"
than the one where detection function is stratified by season.

One downside of the above scheme is that you won't be able to get
density estimates per survey.  With only 10-20 detections per survey
these estimates are unlikely to be reliable in any case.  Also, since
you're interested in season-level inferences, the above scheme assumes
the surveys are evenly spaced through the season, or randomly spaced, or
that animal density varies randomly from survey to survey.  For example,
if there tend to be more birds in one part of the summer and you run
more surveys in that part of the summer, then you won't get the correct
estimate of average summer densities.

I hope this is helpful.

Len Thomas

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Combining Point Surveys
messages.body_plain:
Sorry, my bad for mis-understanding.

I doubt you have enough samples per survey date to get reliable
estimates at that level.  If you're willing to assume that detectability
is constant over the season then fine, but that's quite a strong
assumption.  If the question is about before vs after control event then
you're better to focus at that level.

One option there would be to further stratify into before vs after the
control event, so you have a separate stratum for each season and
before/after control event.  You could then fit a detection function by
stratum, estimate density by stratum, and then compare densities before
vs after the control using a standard statistical test.  If there is a
separate detection function in each stratum then each estimate is
independent apart from the encounter rate dependence caused by the fact
that you re-use sample points between surveys, which you could ignore in
the first instance.  If you do want to take this into account, and are
willing to do the extra work, the most straightforward strategy is to
bootstrap by sample location.  (In case it's helpful, I did something
like this in Durant et al. 2011, citation at the bottom.)

You could also try including before/after control as a covariate in an
MCDS analysis, rather than full stratification of the detection
function.  (In this case, if you're using Distance for Windows, make
sure you tick the option to estimate detection function Globally and by
Stratum in the Estimate tab of the Model Definition).

If you do go the bootstrap route, you could try estimating density by
survey date, and then use the bootstrap to get the appropriate variances
-- e.g., on the difference in average density before vs after the
control, or anything else you're interested in.

Apologies again for mis-understanding the first time.

Cheers, Len

Durant, S., M. Craft, R. Hilborn, S. Bashir, J. Hando and L. Thomas.
2011. Long term trends in carnivore abundance using distance sampling in
Serengeti national park, Tanzania. Journal of Applied Ecology 48:
1490-1500.

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

     I am working on a line transect survey design to estimate bird nest density over a relatively large area (about 716,251 square kilometers). From prior studies, there is some knowledge of the current nest density gradient in the area. I am wondering if it will be beneficial to create several stratum based on the varying levels of density. My understanding of the benefit of this is that it can potentially improve precision of the density estimate because variation in the number of detections between lines within the stratum is lowered. If we are interested in a density estimate at the study area level, not stratum level, would it be okay if there were not 60-80 detections per stratum, but approximately 60-80 when pooling across stratum? And would there also need to be 15-20 replications within each stratum or just pooled across stratum?
     It would also be beneficial if more effort could be focused on the areas of higher density. Does this introduce bias because areas of fewer detections will be confounded with areas of less effort?

     To summarize, my questions are:
     1. When dividing a study area into several stratum, do there need to be a significant number of detections per stratum (60-80) if we are interested only in                 density at the level of the study area (not at the stratum level)? Or is about 60-80 detections when pooled across stratum enough?
     2. When dividing a study area into several stratum, do there need to be 15-20 replicates per stratum if we are interested only in density at the level of the
         study area (not at the stratum level)? Or is 15-20 replicates when pooled across stratum enough?
     3. Does lower effort in stratum with known lower densities produce a bias estimate of density when estimating density for the entire study area?

     Thank you in advance for any interest and input!

-Elaine Gallenberg

messages.body_plain:
Elaine

All valuable things to consider when designing a distance sampling survey.  If you have a copy of Buckland et al. (2015) to hand, have a look at Section 2.3 for a discussion of the subject.

In short, you can use stratification to accomplish one of two purposes: a) estimate density in sub-areas (strata) of your study area or b) increase precision of your estimate across the entire study area as you note.  The suggested sample sizes for number of detections and number of transects applies to the area at which you are performing the estimation, in your case the entire study area.

Regarding effort allocation based upon presumed densities:  it is common to allocate greater effort in areas of higher density.  There are drawbacks to this allocation scheme.  With low effort in areas of low density, estimates of abundance in these areas will be imprecise.  That might not be a problem if the low-density areas are small in size.  But if low density areas are large (high quality habitat is scarce) then these low density areas might constitute a large proportion of the population in the study area (and it will be poorly estimated) (Section 2.3.1 Buckland et al. (2015)).  The result of the effort allocation scheme is unlikely to produce bias in the point estimates, but there the situation as I have described could cause precision to suffer.

If the answer to this question is critical to your investigation, you might consider conducting some contrasting simulations in Distance for Windows or the DSsim R package.
Buckland, S. T., E. A. Rexstad, T. A. Marques, and C. S. Oedekoven. 2015. Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications. Springer.

Diego

You have made a good start with your analysis, but the minimum number of sightings is not a trivial question.  There are a number of things to understand before discussing how sightings influence results.
how many transects were in your survey?
were sightings per km of transect roughly equal across your transects, or were there transects with many sightings and transects with no sightings?
what about the goodness of fit tests of your detection function?
did you truncate data?
did you record groups of deer or deer as individuals, if the former was there variation in group size?
The coefficient of variation you report (which is the ratio of the standard error of the abundance estimate and the abundance estimate itself) is fairly large.  That uncertainty is a combination of uncertainty in the estimated parameters of the detection function, variability in group size and variation in encounter rate between transects.  In line transect estimation, it is the last of these (encounter rate variation) that dominates the overall uncertainty.  This domination can be further heightened if there are few transects; a small number of transects (<15 or 20) will lead to a poor estimate of the variation in encounter rate.  It is this "second" sample size (number of transects) that is under-appreciated and causes difficulty in producing abundance estimates with high reliability.

Then close Distance, perhaps move your .zip file to a new directory location, open the .zip file using Distance and begin afresh.

What may have caused this to begin with?  A wild guess is that you might have the "My Distance Projects" directory being mirrored by Microsoft OneDrive (my computer decided to do that).  If you have a slow internet connection, the file Distance is using might be open when the OneDrive mirroring is taking place; giving rise to the file in use problem.  As I say, just a guess.

See how you get on with a start over.

You might also try to compact your project which might tidy up the project databases and resolve some problems

If you have trouble with the file import, let me know.

I'm not inclined to believe reinstalling the software will alleviate these data issues.

messages.body_plain:
Renan

Thanks for supplying the chi-square goodness of fit table, that helps.   You will notice that in the last distance band (85.7 to 100) you have the second greatest number of detections.  In other words, detectability does not appear to be diminishing as a function of distance for this data set.

Distance sampling assumes that detection probability is a non-increasing function of distance.  If detection probability is high at great distances, then it must also be high at small distances.  Consequently, the Distance software has fit a uniform detection function as best for these data.  This has a horizontal line for a detection function and the same expected values in your chi-square table for all of your distance bands.

I fear the difficulty lies with your data and perhaps field methods for this species.

messages.body_plain:
All

First, thanks to Pierre; I agree with his answer about using species as a covariate (for a reasonable number of species) within the same Distance project.

However, Akashdeep, I do not know of a straightforward way to compute predator carrying capacity based upon abundance of (some) prey.

Likewise Ulises: it is a strong assumption to assert that species have identical detection probabilities.  Detection probabilities depend not only upon the animals, but also upon the observers, field protocols, etc.  A more robust approach would be to analyse data for both species with species as a covariate in the detection function.  Contrast models with and without the species covariate as a way to test the assumption of equality of the detection function.

messages.body_plain:
Sara

You can see from the warning messages that Distance is struggling to fit detection functions to your data.  I have a suspicion that the detection distance histograms do not look "well behaved".  This could be caused by a number of things.  My suspicion is that there are too few detections in one (several) of your size categories.  That is a problem that can easily occur with post-stratification; when not incorporating features of interest into the study design (via stratification) you are left to chance whether your strata groups are going to be adequately represented.

However, rather than requiring each strata to have sufficient detections to fit a detection function, consider using size as a (factor) covariate.  In this way you are using information from all size classes to fit the general shape of the function, with data from each strata used to estimate coefficients that alter the shape of the detection function.  You can continue to use size as a post-stratification criterion, this will permit estimation for each size class.  Is it important that you produce an estimate for each size class?

messages.subject: [distance-sampling] %CV on estimated density and abundance
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
I'm a beginner with distance sampling software though i found it very user friendly and managed to cope with it at some extent. However i have some question to make regarding % coefficient of variation on the estimated density and abundance particularly at "Global level of resolution of estimates"
I have two transect with two species observed from my study site i.e. cattle and puku antelope. Cattle was observed only in one of the transect while puku got observed in all the two transect. So i first estimated density and abundance transect wise to see the estimates using MCDS with habitat categories (factor with four levels) as covariate. With this i got the estimate which i can say "low % CV of density and abundance estimates" presumably the estimates are okay.

I estimated first density of each species per transect i.e. cattle had 34.33%CV on the density and abundance each while puku had 24.195 and 13.11% as CV on transect one and two on density and abundance estimate respectively.

Then, I estimated density and abundance of these two species for the entire study areas in order to deduce an overall density and abundance of them. For cattle's estimates i got  36.34% as a %CV on density and abundance each while puku had  64.62% as %CV on density and abundance each. It can be observed that there's large increase on the  %CV on the estimated parameters (density and abundance) particularly for puku.

My question is, what makes such an  increase in %CV observed when i'm trying to estimate i term it as  an "overall" density and abundance particularly for puku antelope? And is there any way/means to/at least improve the estimates as i guess the large %CV of the estimates will be associated with large standard error thus posing a difficult  moments in deducing the final results particularly ones for puku estimates.

Kind regards
Koggani

messages.body_plain:
Koggani

Your interpretation of analysis and questions about precision indicate you are paying close attention to your findings.

However, rather than discuss the details of your CV comparisons, I'll comment upon your study design.  Your data file and your description indicate your study has only two transects.  With only two transects, it is difficult to make inferences about your entire study area.  It is better to have more short transects scattered throughout the area of interest to make more reliable estimates not only of density or abundance, but also of the precision of those estimates.

Overall uncertainty in estimates of density across a study area stem from two sources: a) uncertainty in the estimates of the detection function parameters and b) variability in encounter rate between transects.  The second of these sources is ignored when density estimates are computed at the transect level; as you did with your first analysis.  The second assessment (for the entire study area) has larger CVs because the between-transect variability in encounter rate is included.

The most common scenario for performing animal surveys is to estimate density or abundance for a study area that is sampled (when using distance sampling) by a number of transects.   Variability in encounters between transects tells a great deal about how variable animal density is across the study area.     (If all transects have the same encounter rate, we conclude animal density is homogeneous.)  You can see that understanding this variability in encounter rates between transects is not possible with only a single transect, and still quite challenging with only two transects.

The answer to your final question about how to improve estimates in your study area is to revisit your survey design replacing few long transects with several short transects.  Perhaps visit our online training materials, concentrating on estimation of precision:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter2/#measures-of-precision

messages.subject: expected cluster size in MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
There is an issue that I have encountered many times. In MCDS I could decide if I wanted it to consider the expected cluster size (using size-biased regression method)  instead of the mean, or only the mean, or the expected given it is significant at an alpha level of 0.15 (or whatever). I can´t see a way in MRDS to take this decision by myself.

I am analyzing some tuna data from aerial survey, stratified in 4 blocks. For example, in block A the mean school size is 872 animals, and the expected size is 496. In block C the mean size is 1425 and the expected is 1745. The differences are huge (and in some cases increasing the school size), which means a huge difference in the final abundance estimate.

Is there any way to deal with this? To tell MRDS in Distance (not using R, but Distance itself) not to increase school size for example, or to only change it at a given alpha level? How can I know the best one to use?

Thanks
Ana Cañadas

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] expected cluster size in MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Ana

The MRDS engine does not have the capacity to interact with the size bias regression computations available in Distance for Windows.  The best way for dealing with possible size bias is to use group size as a covariate in the detection function.

On 31/07/2019 12:43, Ana Cañadas wrote:

> Hi,
> There is an issue that I have encountered many times. In MCDS I could decide if I wanted it to consider the expected cluster size (using size-biased regression method)  instead of the mean, or only the mean, or the expected given it is significant at an alpha level of 0.15 (or whatever). I can´t see a way in MRDS to take this decision by myself.
>
> I am analyzing some tuna data from aerial survey, stratified in 4 blocks. For example, in block A the mean school size is 872 animals, and the expected size is 496. In block C the mean size is 1425 and the expected is 1745. The differences are huge (and in some cases increasing the school size), which means a huge difference in the final abundance estimate.
>
> Is there any way to deal with this? To tell MRDS in Distance (not using R, but Distance itself) not to increase school size for example, or to only change it at a given alpha level? How can I know the best one to use?
>
> Thanks
> Ana Cañadas

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] expected cluster size in MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Ana

With highly variable cluster sizes, it is common to use natural log of cluster size as the covariate.  That natural log could then be standardised to make it even more likely to converge.

See discussion of covariate standardisation in Section 2.2 of  the case study associated with Buckland et al. (2015)

https://synergy.st-andrews.ac.uk/ds-manda/covariates-in-detectability-case-study-hawaiian-amaihi/#adjusting-the-raw-covariates
